question.text: The risk arising from errors in mathematical models used to price and value derivatives is called:

explanation.text: The Logic: Model risk is the risk of loss arising because the mathematical model used to price, value, or hedge a derivative is flawed — wrong assumptions, mis-specified parameters, calibration errors, or limited applicability outside the regime in which it was built. When a model fails to capture real-world market behaviour, the resulting prices and hedges can be materially off, producing unexpected losses. The Trap: Market risk is loss from price movements, operational risk is loss from process/system failures, and systematic risk is non-diversifiable market-wide risk. None of those specifically describe errors inside the pricing model itself, which is what "model risk" denotes. Note: The specific definition of "model risk" as a discrete risk category was not located in the cited NISM-Series-VIII workbook pages (17, 78-79, 202); those pages list counterparty, price, liquidity, legal/regulatory, operational and market risks, and describe option-pricing models without defining "model risk" as a term. The framing above is general industry/regulatory usage of the term rather than a direct workbook citation.
